concepts.name: Article 358 vs Article 359: Automatic Suspension vs Presidential Order
key_dimensions: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 during National Emergency (External Aggression only), whereas Article 359 requires a Presidential Order to suspend specified FRs
Article 358 suspends FR for the entire duration of emergency; Article 359 suspends the right to move courts for enforcement (not the FR itself)
Article 358 applies only to Article 19; Article 359 can apply to any FR except Articles 20 and 21
UPSC trap: Article 359 does NOT apply to Articles 20 and 21 — this is the critical exception often tested

concepts.name: Inviolability of Articles 20 and 21 During Emergency
key_dimensions: Constitutional provision: 44th Amendment Act 1978 made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable even during National Emergency under Article 359
Historical context: During the 1975 Emergency, ADM Jabalpur case allowed suspension of Article 21, which the 44th Amendment corrected
Distinction: Article 20 (Protection against arbitrary conviction) and Article 21 (Right to Life) remain enforceable even when Presidential Order under Article 359 is in operation
UPSC trap: These articles cannot be suspended even by Presidential Order — not even Parliament can authorize this suspension during emergency

concepts.name: Scope and Territorial Application of Article 358
key_dimensions: Article 358 suspends Article 19 FRs only during National Emergency proclaimed on grounds of war or external aggression — NOT armed rebellion (43rd/44th Amendment change)
44th Amendment 1978: Restricted Article 358's automatic operation; now only applies to laws and executive actions 'related to' the emergency
Territorial scope: Article 358 operates across the whole of India, not just the area where emergency is in force (contrast with partial emergency under Article 352)
UPSC trap: Article 358 does NOT apply when emergency is declared on grounds of 'armed rebellion' — only war/external aggression triggers it

concepts.name: Presidential Order Under Article 359: Mechanics and Limitations
key_dimensions: President can issue an order specifying which Fundamental Rights under Part III (except Articles 20 & 21) cannot be enforced during National Emergency
The order must be laid before both Houses of Parliament; it can be revoked by subsequent Presidential Order
The order may apply to the whole territory of India or a specified part thereof
UPSC trap: Article 359 suspends the RIGHT TO MOVE courts, not the Fundamental Right itself — the right technically survives but becomes unenforceable

concepts.name: ADM Jabalpur Case (1976) and Its Overruling in Puttaswamy (2017)
key_dimensions: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla: Supreme Court (4:1) held that during emergency, no person has locus standi to move court for enforcement of Article 21
Justice Khanna's lone dissent argued that Right to Life cannot be suspended even during emergency — later vindicated
Justice D.Y. Chandrachud (Sr.) dissented; his son Justice D.Y. Chandrachud (Jr.) in Puttaswamy (2017) expressly overruled ADM Jabalpur
44th Amendment 1978 constitutionally nullified the ADM Jabalpur ruling by making Articles 20 & 21 non-suspendable

concepts.name: Suspension of Article 19 Freedoms: Scope and Restrictions
key_dimensions: Article 19 guarantees six freedoms (speech, assembly, movement, residence, profession, etc.); all six are suspended under Article 358 during external emergency
During Article 358 suspension, State can make any law or take any executive action abridging Article 19 rights without being challenged as unconstitutional
Post-44th Amendment: Even under Article 358, only those laws and actions that have a 'nexus' with the emergency can override Article 19
UPSC trap: Article 19 is NOT suspended during President's Rule (Article 356) or Financial Emergency (Article 360) — only National Emergency triggers Article 358

concepts.name: National Emergency Under Article 352: Grounds and Types
key_dimensions: Three grounds: War, External Aggression, and Armed Rebellion (term 'internal disturbance' replaced by 'armed rebellion' by 44th Amendment)
Proclamation can be issued even before actual occurrence of war/aggression/rebellion if President is satisfied about imminent danger
44th Amendment raised procedural bar: Cabinet must advise in writing; Lok Sabha must approve by special majority within one month
UPSC trap: Emergency due to 'armed rebellion' does NOT automatically suspend Article 19 under Article 358 — this distinction is a classic UPSC trap

concepts.name: 44th Constitutional Amendment Act 1978: Safeguards Against Emergency Misuse
key_dimensions: Changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' as a ground — raising the threshold for emergency proclamation
Made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable under Article 359 — direct response to ADM Jabalpur case
Restricted Article 358 to only war/external aggression emergencies and required nexus of law/action with emergency
Introduced safeguard: Lok Sabha can pass resolution by simple majority to revoke emergency; President must revoke upon such resolution

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Emergency Proclamation and FR Suspension
key_dimensions: Minerva Mills (1980): Supreme Court held that judicial review is a basic feature of the Constitution; emergency proclamation can be judicially reviewed on grounds of mala fide or irrelevant grounds
38th Amendment (1975) which made emergency non-justiciable was struck down as unconstitutional in Minerva Mills
Courts can examine whether the Presidential satisfaction is based on relevant material, even during emergency
UPSC trap: While courts can review the proclamation, they apply a limited standard of review (not full merits review) — 'satisfaction' of President is subjective but not immune

concepts.name: Habeas Corpus During Emergency: Historical and Constitutional Analysis
key_dimensions: Habeas Corpus (Article 32/226) is a remedy under Article 21; its suspension during emergency was the core issue in ADM Jabalpur
Post-44th Amendment: Since Article 21 cannot be suspended, Habeas Corpus remains available even during National Emergency
Article 359 suspends right to move courts under Article 32 (not Article 226) — High Courts can still hear Habeas Corpus petitions under Article 226 even if Article 32 is suspended
UPSC trap: Article 359 order suspends enforcement under Article 32 but High Courts retain power under Article 226 (though 44th Amendment empowered Parliament to restrict this)

concepts.name: President's Rule (Article 356) and Its Effect on Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Article 356 (President's Rule in States) does NOT automatically suspend any Fundamental Rights — no equivalent of Articles 358 or 359 applies
Under President's Rule, Parliament can legislate on state subjects but such laws cannot violate FRs
Citizens retain all FRs including Article 19, 21, 32 during President's Rule — a common misconception tested by UPSC
UPSC trap: Students often confuse President's Rule with National Emergency — only National Emergency can lead to FR suspension, not Article 356

concepts.name: Financial Emergency (Article 360) and Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Financial Emergency under Article 360 does NOT suspend any Fundamental Rights — neither Article 358 nor Article 359 is triggered
Under Financial Emergency, President can direct states to observe financial propriety; salaries of civil servants and judges can be reduced
Article 360 has never been proclaimed in India's history
UPSC trap: Financial Emergency has NO provision for FR suspension — a standard distractor in MCQs asking which emergency affects FRs

concepts.name: Preventive Detention Laws and Suspension of Article 22 Rights
key_dimensions: Article 22 provides safeguards against arrest but also explicitly authorizes preventive detention laws (Articles 22(4) to 22(7))
During National Emergency, Parliament can enact preventive detention laws for longer periods than normally permitted under Article 22
MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act) during 1975 Emergency was used with Article 359 order suspending Articles 21 and 22 enforcement
UPSC trap: Preventive detention safeguards (Article 22(4)-(7)) can be curtailed during emergency, but post-44th Amendment, Article 21 core cannot be abridged

concepts.name: Partial Emergency and Geographic Scope of FR Suspension
key_dimensions: After 42nd Amendment: Emergency can be proclaimed for a part of India's territory, not necessarily the whole country
When emergency is confined to a part of India, Article 358 and 359 effects are also limited to that territory
This creates a scenario where some citizens may have Article 19 suspended while others in non-emergency areas retain full rights
UPSC angle: Partial emergency tests understanding of territorial application of constitutional provisions — relatively less discussed but UPSC has tested this

concepts.name: Suspension vs. Abridgement vs. Waiver of Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Suspension: Temporary non-enforceability during emergency; FR technically exists but cannot be enforced in courts
Abridgement: Reasonable restrictions under Articles 19(2)-(6), 25(2), etc. — permanent regulatory limitations, not suspension
Waiver: Supreme Court held in Behram Khurshid Pesikaka that FRs cannot be waived by individuals since they serve public interest
UPSC trap: Article 359 creates 'suspension of enforcement' not suspension of the right itself — this philosophical distinction is critical

concepts.name: Role of Parliament During Emergency in Relation to FR Legislation
key_dimensions: During National Emergency, Parliament can legislate on State List subjects (Article 250) but such laws cannot violate FRs (unless FRs are suspended)
Parliament by law under Article 359(1A) can also extend Article 359 suspension to High Court proceedings under Article 226
Laws made during emergency that abridge Article 19 cease to have effect six months after emergency ends (Article 358(2))
UPSC trap: Executive actions taken during emergency that abridge Article 19 also become void six months after emergency — not just legislative actions

concepts.name: Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) During Emergency
key_dimensions: Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right; it can be suspended by Presidential Order under Article 359 (unlike Articles 20 & 21)
Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' — its suspension is thus extraordinary
When Article 32 is suspended under Article 359, citizens can still approach High Courts under Article 226 (writ jurisdiction)
UPSC trap: Article 32 can be suspended; Article 226 (High Court writ) cannot be suspended by Article 359 — Parliament needs separate law for that

concepts.name: Effect of Emergency on State Autonomy and FR vis-à-vis State Action
key_dimensions: During National Emergency, Parliament can give directions to States; State governments remain in office but act under Parliamentary supremacy
FRs against State action (Articles 12-35) remain applicable to State action during emergency except where specifically suspended
Article 13 (laws inconsistent with FRs are void) continues to operate except where Article 358 or 359 orders create exceptions
UPSC angle: Often tested whether States can independently abridge FRs during emergency — they cannot unless Parliamentary law or Presidential direction authorizes it

concepts.name: Comparison: Emergency Provisions in India vs. Other Constitutions
key_dimensions: Unlike USA (no explicit emergency suspension provision), India has elaborate Articles 352-360 codifying emergency powers
UK relies on convention and parliamentary sovereignty; India's written constitution provides structured but limited FR suspension

International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) Article 4 allows derogation during public emergency but never permits suspension of right to life — mirrors India's post-44th Amendment position
UPSC Mains angle: India's framework is more structured than most democracies but 1975 Emergency showed structural vulnerabilities addressed by 44th Amendment

concepts.name: Post-Emergency Accountability: Validity of Actions Taken During Suspension
key_dimensions: Laws made during emergency under Article 358 that abridge Article 19 automatically become inoperative six months after emergency ends
Executive actions taken during emergency that violated Article 19 cannot be challenged during emergency but can be questioned after
Shah Commission (1977) investigated excesses during 1975-77 Emergency — highlighted need for accountability mechanisms
UPSC trap: The 'six-month' survival clause for laws post-emergency is frequently tested; executive actions do not get this six-month grace period under Article 358(2)
